grounds.point: Section 14(1)(b) permits eviction where the tenant has sub-let, assigned or otherwise parted with possession of the whole or part of the premises without the landlord's written consent.
grounds.explanation: The supplied statutory text expressly identifies sub-letting, assignment and otherwise parting with possession after 9 June 1952 without written landlord consent as grounds for recovery of possession. The fixed target dispute was narrowed to parting with possession rather than subletting.

grounds.point: The Rent Control Tribunal found, and the High Court accepted, that Duli Chand had parted with the legal possession of the tenanted shop.
grounds.explanation: The Tribunal expressly found parting with legal possession and ordered eviction under section 14(1)(b), and the High Court confirmed that finding. These are prior-court findings preserved in the allowed record, not merely the landlord's allegation.

grounds.point: Sri Bhagwan exclusively possessed the shop and operated his own sole-proprietary business there, while Duli Chand had no interest in that business and retained no control over the premises.
grounds.explanation: The Tribunal findings accepted by the High Court state that Sri Bhagwan was the sole proprietor, carried on his business in the premises, and had exclusive possession, while Duli Chand worked elsewhere, had no business interest, and retained no control. Occasional sightings of Duli Chand sitting in the shop do not erase the express findings of exclusive possession and absence of retained control; the supplied reported Delhi-law passage also describes section 14(b) as broadly extending beyond subleases to assignment or other modes of parting with possession.

grounds.point: No written consent from the landlord for the parting with possession was pleaded or shown in the allowed record.
grounds.explanation: The landlord's petition alleged that the transfer of possession occurred without written consent, and the court expressly recorded that the tenant never pleaded that he had obtained written consent. It consequently treated whether possession had been parted with as the only remaining question, so the allowed record supplies no competing consent basis defeating clause (b).

grounds.point: Sri Bhagwan's status as Duli Chand's natural son does not displace the preserved findings that Sri Bhagwan had exclusive possession and Duli Chand retained no control.
grounds.explanation: The tenant relied on the father-son relationship and disputed a valid adoption, while the supplied record notes the adoption-law argument. But the operative possession findings independently state exclusive possession by Sri Bhagwan and lack of retained control by Duli Chand; none of the supplied Delhi statutory text creates a family-member exception that overrides those findings.

reason: On the supplied record, the statutory elements material to the fixed ground are supported: prior courts found that the tenant parted with legal possession, the underlying findings show exclusive possession by Sri Bhagwan and no retained control by the tenant, and no written landlord consent was pleaded or shown. Within the limits of the supplied law, those findings support eviction under section 14(1)(b) without requiring a determination that there was a sublease or a valid adoption.
